## 146. How many times per hour do the sun's rays hit Earth?

The answer depends on what you mean by “rays.” If you are talking about photons, then they come in at all frequencies of the electromagnetic spectrum and with every direction (except exactly into the Sun’s center) as long as it is not in daylight. So we could say that there are $2\pi$ rays per unit time from the sun hitting Earth for each hemisphere: one coming from above, one below.

If you mean a ray of white sunlight, then the answer is two rays. During daytime, most photons come with enough energy to escape the atmosphere; only those below $\lambda \approx 400 \mathrm{~nm}$ are absorbed by ozone (see Figure 16.23). Since blue light has wavelengths between $400$ and $700 \mathrm{~nm}$, it is what we see as sunlight. But red, orange, green, yellow, etc. all have longer wavelengths and pass through the atmosphere unaffected. When you look at a white object from directly overhead in midday, the sun appears to be a bright disk of pure white light; but your eyes are actually seeing only blue photons.
